source.title: Variable Mini-Batch Sizing and Pre-Trained Embeddings
source.authors: Mostafa Abdou; Vladan Gloncak; Ondrej Bojar

record.tranche_reason: Tests changing mini-batch size during English-to-Czech neural machine translation, an application beyond the image classifiers and language models named in V5.
record.gate_note: The paper reports held-out BLEU results for batch-size changes. The embedding analysis and cited prior work are not results on the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study uses the small-batch generalization finding to motivate variable batch-size schedules, but reports those schedules' performance rather than testing V5's fixed-epoch large-versus-small batch comparison. Training is scheduled by wall-clock time, and the baseline and incrementation run remain unconverged. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the tested techniques did not improve performance, except that batch-size incrementation slightly increased wall-clock training speed through better GPU use. The authors also conclude that decrementation harmed both training and held-out performance.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies batch size during NMT training rather than comparing fixed large and small batches under a fixed epoch budget.
record.method_sensitivity: For decrementation, reducing the batch size more often led to earlier performance loss. The incrementation run showed a small wall-clock learning-speed gain but no observable difference by training steps.

fits_no_version.finding: More frequent batch-size reductions produced earlier held-out performance loss; the authors also report declining training performance and interpret this as impaired learning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reducing batch size during ongoing NMT training can impair optimization and held-out translation performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing batch size from 65 to 100 after one week slightly improved wall-clock learning speed, with no observable difference by examples processed.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A mid-training batch-size increase can improve computational throughput without improving learning efficiency per example.

record.problems: The authors report resource limits and say the baseline was not fully converged. They could not run pairs of directly comparable embedding setups. The mini-batch outcomes are shown in plots without numerical held-out scores or uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No other batch-size rows were left out. The embedding results do not bear on the listed versions.

untested.parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization in the same architectures and training recipes.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizers and dependence on tuning.
Large-versus-small batch held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets, workload-dependent thresholds, and recipe changes that remove a demonstrated penalty.
Dropout interventions and their dependence on dataset size, dropout strength, or augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization gaps, and comparisons with alternative measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus removing equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The unsuccessful decreasing-batch schedules do not challenge V5: V5 does not predict that decreasing batch size mid-training must improve performance. The baseline's reported BLEU of 15.24 is after two weeks, not an equal-epoch comparator for the schedules.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and generalization on natural labels.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Comparisons of adaptive and non-adaptive optimizers.
Fixed-epoch comparisons of large and small batches; image classifiers and language models; the text gives no numerical held-out scores for the batch-size experiments.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the train-test gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring test accuracy.

rows.subject: Decrease every 12h
rows.operation_detail: Decreased mini-batch size during training, starting at 100 and reaching 5.
rows.value: The model starts losing performance sooner as the mini-batch size is reduced more often.
rows.note: The paper describes the trend across the decrementation experiments but gives no separate numerical held-out value for this run.
rows.check: The reported performance decline concerns reducing batch size during training, not comparing large and small batches under equal epoch budgets. It cannot establish a reversal of V5.

rows.subject: Decrease every 24h
rows.operation_detail: Decreased mini-batch size during training, starting at 100 and reaching 5.
rows.value: The model starts losing performance sooner as the mini-batch size is reduced more often.
rows.note: The paper describes the trend across the decrementation experiments but gives no separate numerical held-out value for this run.
rows.check: The reported performance decline concerns reducing batch size during training, not comparing large and small batches under equal epoch budgets. It cannot establish a reversal of V5.

rows.subject: Decrease every 48h
rows.operation_detail: Decreased mini-batch size during training, starting at 150 and reaching 20.
rows.value: Reducing mini-batch size during training led to a loss on the held-out dataset.
rows.note: The paper identifies this as its primary submission.
rows.check: This schedule does not test V5's fixed-epoch comparison. The starting batch size is internally inconsistent: Table 3 gives 150, whereas Section 3.1 gives 100. Section 4.1 reports declining training and held-out performance, so the result does not isolate a generalization penalty.

rows.subject: Increase every 12h
rows.operation_detail: Trained for a week with mini-batch size 65, then increased it to 100 for another week.
rows.note: The figure plots held-out performance, but the text reports only a very small gain in learning speed and no observable difference in training steps.
rows.check: The subject label is misleading: Section 3.2 describes one increase from 65 to 100 after a week, not increases every 12 hours. The text explicitly reports slight outperformance in wall-clock learning speed and no observable difference by examples processed; neither comparison tests V5 under equal epoch budgets.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Mini-batch decrementation during English-to-Czech NMT training
reader_labels.reason: Decrementing the batch size led to worse held-out performance as well as worse training performance (R1–R3), so this schedule did not improve generalization in the tested setting.
